copy.blurb:
A +3.6pp gap on the the draw side. Brazil v Haiti in FIFA World Cup 2026 is the match. The model has the draw stronger than the market does — that's the reason this fires as a Pick rather than a Pass.

On Elo, Brazil comes in 520 points ahead — Brazil at 1970, Haiti at 1450. Both Elo numbers are pulled live from the public Elo source. The adjustment layer is quiet on this fixture — no host bonus, no home-ground correction, no altitude folding in. The Elo numbers above are what the model uses.

Three-way split from the model: Brazil to win at 86%, the draw at 10%, and Haiti to win at 4%. The draw side reads 10% on this distribution — the model's central case for the draw.

On the same three-way, Polymarket: Brazil to win at 92%, the draw at 6%, and Haiti to win at 3%. On the the draw side specifically the market reads 6%, which prices out at American odds of +1475. Compared against the model's 10%, that's the +3.6pp gap the Pick rests on.

Pick gate is a lower-bound check, not the point estimate. A 100-sample bootstrap perturbs the Elo prior (±20), the host bonus (±15), and the altitude bonus (±10), then reads the 5th-percentile probability back out. On the the draw side that lower bound is 10% — +3.7pp clear of the market's 6%, comfortably past our +3pp threshold. The point is selection, not a blanket call. Most matches the model and the market agree on. This is one of the ones where they don't, and the gap is on the the draw side specifically.

This number will move. The confirmed starting eleven, fitness news, weather at the venue, and any tournament suspension carried in from previous matches all feed back into the prior. With kickoff 24 days out, refresh is weekly; daily cadence picks up inside the final five days. A wide Pick can collapse into a Pass if news moves enough of the read.
